title: Named Boxes (Variables)
story: You're filling out a profile card for a new social app. Instead of writing your name over and over in every field, you write it once at the top and refer to it. Programming works the same way — you store a value in a named box once, then use the name whenever you need it.
why: Variables are how programs remember things. Without them, every time you needed a piece of information — your name, your score, your high score — you'd have to retype it from scratch.
analogy: A variable is like a labeled box — you put something inside and give it a name so you can find it later.
try_it: Add a variable for your favorite food and print it. Then add a variable for your favorite number. Can you print them all in one program?
tips: Use `let` to create a variable — think of it as 'let this box hold this value.'
When printing a variable, don't use quotes: `io.println(name)` prints the value, while `io.println("name")` prints the word 'name'.
Variable names should describe what's inside: `age`, `score`, `favorite_color` are good. `x`, `a`, `stuff` are confusing.
XIOM figures out the type automatically — you can write `let age = 14` without saying it's a number.
common_mistakes: Putting a variable name in quotes: `io.println("name")` prints the text 'name', not the value inside the variable.
Using a variable before creating it with `let` — you must create the box before you can look inside it.
Putting spaces in variable names: `high score` is not allowed. Use `high_score` instead.
Starting a variable name with a number: `1st_place` won't work. Use `first_place` instead.
